# /live-dashboard — Build a Live Operations Cockpit

You are building an **operations cockpit**: one self-contained HTML
artifact the person re-opens every day. On open it fetches fresh data
from their connected MCP tools through the artifact's tool bridge,
renders it as an operator dashboard, and drives a **human-in-the-loop**
review workflow — the person reviews, edits, approves, and only then
does anything go out.

The dashboard is the operator's cockpit, not a robot. Drafting proposes;
the human disposes. Nothing sends or writes to an external system until
the human approves it, unless the person has explicitly told you a
specific category is safe to auto-send.

This skill is **connector-agnostic**. Do NOT assume any particular
company, product, or tool set. The person tells you what they want to
run and which tools they have; you discover the real shape of those
tools and build to fit. The worked examples below name real connectors
(Supabase, Gmail, Google Calendar, Attio, Leadbay) only as concrete
anchors for the trickier parsing — lift the *method*, not the tool name.

## The Iron Laws (NON-NEGOTIABLE)

These are the laws that, if broken, make the cockpit dangerous — it
sends something the human never sanctioned, or ships a confident lie.

1. **Human-approved by default for anything outbound or destructive.**
   Sending an email, writing to an external system, deleting, updating a
   record — all HELD until the human explicitly approves, unless the
   person named that exact category as safe to auto-send. Read is free;
   write and send are gated.
2. **Discovery before building.** Call each connected tool ONCE and read
   its real parameters and real response shape BEFORE you write a single
   line of parsing. MCP wrappers rename fields and reshape output. Build
   around what you observed, never around what you assumed.
3. **Decouple drafting from sending.** Drafting produces a queued item.
   A separate, explicit sender acts on approved items. The drafting path
   must be structurally incapable of sending anything by itself.
4. **Never invent facts.** No made-up availability, prices, commitments,
   links, names, or numbers in any draft. If a fact is needed and
   unverifiable, HOLD the item and flag it for the human — do not guess
   or ship a placeholder.
5. **Leave authoritative systems to their owners.** If a CRM (or any
   system) is kept in sync by a real sync job, the cockpit reads from it;
   it does not become a second writer racing that job. Default read-only
   there.
6. **Idempotent by construction.** Every send/write is deduped so a
   double-click, a reload, or a re-run cannot double-send. Track what has
   already acted and refuse to act twice.

If any law would be broken to satisfy a request, STOP and surface it —
don't quietly relax a law to get the demo working.

## Phase 0 — Understand the job and propose connectors

Do NOT start building. First learn two things: **what operation** the
person runs, and **which tools** they have connected.

### 0a. Understand the operation

Ask, in plain terms:
- What do you do every day that this dashboard should show you and help
  you act on? (e.g. "clear my inbox", "review outreach before it goes
  out", "see my pipeline and what's stalled")
- What decisions do YOU want to keep making, and what's safe to let the
  dashboard prepare for you?
- What must NEVER happen automatically?

The answers set the whole design: the categories in the review queue,
which are auto-send vs HELD, and what counts as "needs the human".

### 0b. Inventory what's actually connected

Look at the tools available in this session. Group them by role — this
is the connector palette for an operations cockpit:

| Role | Purpose in the cockpit | Example connectors |
|---|---|---|
| **Hub (database)** | Central store: queue, learning log, dedup ledger, cached snapshots | Supabase / Postgres |
| **Inbox + outbound** | Read messages to triage, prepare drafts, send on approval | Gmail |
| **Calendar** | Meetings, availability, "booked" signals | Google Calendar |
| **CRM** | Contact + stage/pipeline data (read; owned by its sync job) | Attio, HubSpot, Salesforce |
| **Data / lead source** | New records to work, enrichment, research | Leadbay |

Propose the smallest set that covers the person's job. A cockpit almost
always wants a **hub database** — it holds the review queue, the dedup
ledger, and the learning log so state survives reloads and the dashboard
isn't re-deriving everything from scratch each open. If they have no
database connected, say so and offer to set one up (Supabase is the easy
default), because without it the queue and dedup are fragile.

Use AskUserQuestion to confirm the connector set and the job before
building. If a needed connector isn't connected, name it and ask them to
connect it (most of these expose an `authenticate` tool you can point
them at) rather than working around the gap.

## Phase 1 — Discovery: probe each tool ONCE (Iron Law #2)

This is the phase people skip and regret. MCP wrappers do not return what
the underlying API docs say. They rename fields, wrap payloads in
envelopes, and — critically — **often return the real data as a JSON
string nested inside a text envelope**, not as structured JSON.

For each tool the cockpit will call, invoke it once with a minimal real
argument and record:
- the exact **parameter names** it accepts (not what you'd guess),
- the exact **response envelope** (where the payload actually lives),
- whether the payload is structured JSON or a **stringified** blob you
  must `JSON.parse` a second time,
- the field names on each record (wrappers rename `email` → `emailAddress`,
  `id` → `record_id`, etc.).

Write these observations down — they are the spec your artifact parses
against. A one-line-per-tool "observed shape" note is enough.

### Worked example — the envelopes you'll actually meet

**Supabase `execute_sql`** commonly returns the rows as a JSON string
inside a text content block:

```jsonc
{
  "content": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "[{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"Acme\",\"stage\":\"lead\"}]" }
  ]
}
// The rows are content[0].text — a STRING. You must JSON.parse it again.
```

**A CRM list (Attio-style)** may wrap records and rename the id:

```jsonc
{
  "content": [
    { "type": "text", "text": "{\"data\":[{\"id\":{\"record_id\":\"abc\"},\"values\":{\"name\":[{\"value\":\"Acme\"}]}}]}" }
  ]
}
// Real records at JSON.parse(content[0].text).data
// The name is values.name[0].value — NOT record.name.
```

**Gmail search** may return threads with ids you then hydrate with a
second `get_thread` / `get_message` call — discovery tells you whether
the search already includes the body or just the id.

The lesson generalises: **never trust the field path; observe it.** Build
a single tolerant parser (Phase 2) that copes with all of these.

## Phase 2 — The live data layer inside the artifact

Now build the artifact. Everything below is inline in ONE self-contained
HTML file. Fetch on open through the tool bridge, cache the result, and
offer a manual reload. Light mode, approved CDNs only, no external calls
except the tool bridge.

### 2a. Wait for the bridge, then fetch

The tool bridge (`window.claude` / the artifact's callTool) may not be
ready the instant the page paints. Wait for it, then fetch with per-query
retry and backoff. Cache the parsed result so views read from memory, not
from a re-fetch.

```js
// --- bridge readiness -------------------------------------------------
async function waitForBridge(timeoutMs = 8000) {
  const start = Date.now();
  while (!window.claude || typeof window.claude.callTool !== "function") {
    if (Date.now() - start > timeoutMs) throw new Error("Tool bridge never became available");
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 100));
  }
  return window.claude;
}

// --- one tool call, with retry + backoff ------------------------------
async function callToolRetry(name, args, { tries = 3, baseMs = 400 } = {}) {
  let lastErr;
  for (let i = 0; i < tries; i++) {
    try {
      const bridge = await waitForBridge();
      return await bridge.callTool(name, args);
    } catch (e) {
      lastErr = e;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, baseMs * 2 ** i)); // 400, 800, 1600ms
    }
  }
  throw lastErr;
}
```

### 2b. Tolerant result parsing (the double-parse problem)

Results arrive in envelopes, and the real payload is often a JSON string.
One parser handles every shape you observed in Phase 1:

```js
// Pull the meaningful payload out of ANY MCP result envelope.
// Handles: raw object, {content:[{text}]}, and stringified-JSON-in-text.
function parseToolResult(res) {
  if (res == null) return null;

  // Some bridges hand back the value directly.
  if (typeof res === "object" && !("content" in res) && !("text" in res)) {
    // Already structured (array or plain object).
    return res;
  }

  // Extract the text envelope if present.
  let text = null;
  if (typeof res === "string") text = res;
  else if (Array.isArray(res?.content)) {
    text = res.content.map(c => c?.text ?? "").join("");
  } else if (typeof res?.text === "string") {
    text = res.text;
  }
  if (text == null) return res; // give the caller the raw thing to inspect

  // The text is very often itself JSON. Try to parse; fall back to raw text.
  const t = text.trim();
  if (t.startsWith("{") || t.startsWith("[")) {
    try { return JSON.parse(t); } catch { /* not JSON after all */ }
  }
  return text;
}

// Convenience: call + parse in one step.
async function query(name, args, opts) {
  return parseToolResult(await callToolRetry(name, args, opts));
}
```

### 2c. Cache on load, offer reload

```js
const STATE = { data: {}, loadedAt: null };

async function loadAll() {
  setStatus("Loading…");
  // Run the fetches you designed in Phase 0/1. Example:
  const [rows, threads, events] = await Promise.all([
    query("Supabase__execute_sql", { query: "select * from queue where status <> 'sent'" }),
    query("Gmail__search_threads", { q: "in:inbox newer_than:7d" }),
    query("Google_Calendar__list_events", { timeMin: new Date().toISOString() }),
  ]);
  STATE.data = { rows, threads, events };
  STATE.loadedAt = new Date();
  render();
  setStatus(`Loaded ${STATE.loadedAt.toLocaleTimeString()}`);
}

document.getElementById("reload").addEventListener("click", loadAll);
window.addEventListener("load", () => loadAll().catch(showError));
```

Guard every render against the empty and error states — a cockpit that
shows a blank white box on a failed fetch is worse than one that says
"couldn't load calendar — retry".

## Phase 3 — Dashboard view toolbox

Build only the views the person's job needs. Self-contained, light mode,
approved CDNs only. The palette:

- **KPI stat cards** — a row of big-number cards (count today, awaiting
  approval, sent, held). One glance = state of the operation.
- **Sortable / filterable tables** — click a header to sort; a filter bar
  above. Persist the sort + filter choice (Phase 9).
- **Pipeline / kanban board** — columns by stage, cards draggable or
  read-only, **collapsible columns** so a busy board stays scannable.
- **Activity heatmap / sparklines** — small inline SVG; volume over the
  last N days. No charting CDN needed for a sparkline — draw an SVG
  polyline yourself.
- **Collapsible sections + filter bars** — group the dashboard so the
  operator opens only what they're working.

Keep it operator-friendly: dense where it helps scanning, roomy where a
decision is made. The review queue (Phase 4) is the part they live in —
give it the most care.

## Phase 4 — The review / approval queue (the heart of it)

This is the reason the cockpit exists. Items are grouped into
**categories**. Per category, the person decides the policy: **auto-send**
(safe, high-confidence, they opted in) or **HELD** (needs their explicit
approval). HELD is the default for anything you're unsure about.

Every row supports: **preview**, **inline edit** (click the item itself —
Phase 9), **approve**, **send now**, **stop/skip**, and **bulk actions**
across a selection. Approved-vs-pending state is always visible. **A HELD
item never acts until the human approves it.**

The structural rule (Iron Law #3): the queue holds *intent*; a separate
sender acts on *approved intent*. Drafting writes to the queue and stops.

```js
// A queue item is data, never an action. status drives everything.
// status: "held" | "approved" | "sending" | "sent" | "skipped" | "failed"
function makeItem({ id, category, policy, to, subject, body, context }) {
  return {
    id,                    // stable, content-derived — powers dedup (Phase 10)
    category, policy,      // policy: "auto" | "held"
    to, subject, body,
    context,               // why this exists: the source msg, the signal
    status: policy === "auto" ? "approved" : "held",
    approvedAt: null, sentAt: null, error: null,
  };
}

// The SENDER is the only thing that calls an outbound tool. It refuses
// to touch anything that isn't approved, and dedups against the ledger.
async function sendApproved(items) {
  for (const it of items.filter(i => i.status === "approved")) {
    if (await alreadySent(it.id)) { it.status = "sent"; continue; } // idempotent
    it.status = "sending"; render();
    try {
      // Outbound tool call — the ONE place a send happens.
      await callToolRetry("Gmail__create_draft", buildSendArgs(it)); // or send, per policy
      await recordSent(it.id);          // write to dedup ledger in the hub DB
      it.status = "sent"; it.sentAt = new Date();
    } catch (e) {
      it.status = "failed"; it.error = String(e);
    }
    render();
  }
}
```

Notice: `sendApproved` filters to `approved`. A `held` item is
structurally unreachable by the sender until a human action flips it to
`approved`. That's the guarantee, encoded in code, not in a comment.

Default the outbound call to **creating a draft** (reversible) rather than
sending, unless the person explicitly opted a category into true send.
Reversibility keeps the cost of being wrong low.

## Phase 5 — Drafting / outbound preparation

When you prepare an outbound message, prepare it in the **person's own
voice**, and preserve the mechanics of a real reply:

- **Preserve signature / footer** — carry the person's existing signature;
  don't invent one.
- **Preserve the quoted original** — when replying, keep the quoted thread
  below the new text so context travels with it.
- **Thread correctly** — reply on the right thread with the right
  `In-Reply-To` / references (discovery in Phase 1 tells you the fields);
  don't start a new thread for a reply.
- **Never invent facts** (Iron Law #4) — no availability you didn't
  confirm from the calendar, no price, no commitment, no link you can't
  verify. Missing a needed fact → HOLD and flag (Phase 7).

The draft lands in the queue as a HELD item (unless the category is
opted into auto). It does not send.

## Phase 6 — Classification / triage

To decide what belongs in the queue, scan the source (e.g. the inbox) and
classify each item. A useful default taxonomy:

- **needs a reply** — a real ask waiting on the person → draft + queue.
- **already handled** — the person (or the thread) already answered → skip.
- **meeting booked** — calendar confirms it → surface, no reply needed.
- **objection** — needs judgment → HELD with the context, never auto.
- **noise** — newsletters, receipts, automated → filtered out of the
  cockpit entirely.

**Dedup against what's already been answered** — check the thread and the
dedup ledger before drafting, so you never queue a reply to something the
person already dealt with. Surface **only what genuinely needs them**,
and give each surfaced item a ready draft plus the context behind it (the
triggering message, the signal, the record) so they can decide in
seconds without leaving the cockpit.

Classification is a good use of AI-in-the-artifact (Phase 8): send the
message text to `askClaude` with the taxonomy and let it label + explain.

## Phase 7 — Flag for human (don't guess, HOLD)

Whenever an item can't be completed **safely**, HOLD it and flag it
clearly as needing human input. The triggers:

- a **missing asset or link** (the draft needs a deck / URL you don't
  have),
- an **unverifiable fact** (a date, price, or claim you can't confirm),
- a **decision only the human can make** (pricing, a commitment, a
  relationship call).

The flag is a first-class state, visible in the row, with a one-line
reason ("held: needs the pricing PDF link"). It is NEVER a placeholder
shipped as if real, and NEVER a guess. A flagged item is a good outcome —
it means the cockpit knew its limits.

## Phase 8 — AI inside the artifact + the learning loop

The artifact can call the model on demand through an `askClaude`-style
bridge call. Use it for:

- **summaries** — collapse a long thread into two lines of context on the
  row,
- **classification** — the triage labels in Phase 6,
- **"regenerate this draft with my feedback"** — a control on each row:
  the person types "warmer, and mention we met at the conf", you
  regenerate.

```js
async function askClaude(prompt, { system } = {}) {
  const bridge = await waitForBridge();
  // Shape mirrors the tool bridge; discover the exact method name in Phase 1.
  const res = await bridge.complete
    ? bridge.complete({ prompt, system })
    : bridge.callTool("claude__complete", { prompt, system });
  return parseToolResult(await res);
}

async function regenerateDraft(item, feedback) {
  const style = await loadStyleExamples();      // see the learning loop below
  const next = await askClaude(
    `Rewrite this draft applying the feedback. Keep the signature and the
     quoted original. Invent no facts.\n\nFEEDBACK: ${feedback}\n\nDRAFT:\n${item.body}`,
    { system: `Match this person's voice. Examples of their edits:\n${style}` }
  );
  item.body = String(next);
  render();
}
```

### The learning loop

Every time the person edits a draft before approving, log the
**before/after** pair to a table in the hub database. Feed recent pairs
back into the drafting system prompt so future drafts drift toward their
style. Cheap, compounding, and it makes the cockpit feel like it's
learning them.

```js
async function logEdit(item, before, after) {
  if (before === after) return;                 // no lesson in a no-op
  await callToolRetry("Supabase__execute_sql", {
    query: `insert into draft_edits (item_id, category, before_text, after_text, created_at)
            values ($1,$2,$3,$4, now())`,
    params: [item.id, item.category, before, after],
  });
}

async function loadStyleExamples(limit = 20) {
  const rows = await query("Supabase__execute_sql", {
    query: `select before_text, after_text from draft_edits
            order by created_at desc limit ${limit}`,
  });
  return (Array.isArray(rows) ? rows : [])
    .map(r => `BEFORE: ${r.before_text}\nAFTER: ${r.after_text}`).join("\n---\n");
}
```

## Phase 9 — UX polish

Small things that make it feel like a real tool, not a report:

- **Click the item to edit it** — the row/card itself is the edit affordance,
  not a separate pencil button. Click → it becomes editable in place.
- **Click-outside to close / commit** — clicking away from an open editor
  closes it (and commits, logging the edit via `logEdit`).
- **Toasts for feedback** — every action (approved, sent, held, failed)
  fires a short toast. The operator never wonders whether the click
  registered.
- **Persist view state** — sort column, filter selection, collapsed
  sections, active category. Save to `localStorage` (or the hub DB for
  cross-device) so re-opening lands them where they left off.

```js
// Persist and restore view preferences.
const VIEW_KEY = "cockpit.view.v1";
function saveView(v) { localStorage.setItem(VIEW_KEY, JSON.stringify(v)); }
function loadView() { try { return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(VIEW_KEY)) || {}; } catch { return {}; } }

// Click-outside to commit an open inline editor.
document.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const open = document.querySelector(".editing");
  if (open && !open.contains(e.target)) commitEditor(open);
});
```

## Phase 10 — Guardrails and the scheduled prep job

Bring the Iron Laws home in the build:

- **Read-only / human-approved by default** for anything outbound or
  destructive. Auto-send only for categories the person explicitly opted
  in.
- **Leave authoritative systems to their sync jobs.** Read the CRM; don't
  become a second writer. If the cockpit must reflect a stage change, do
  it through the owning path, not a raw write that races the sync.
- **Idempotency / dedup ledger.** A `sent` table keyed by the item's
  stable id. `alreadySent(id)` checks it before every send; `recordSent(id)`
  writes after. A reload or double-click cannot double-send.

```js
async function alreadySent(id) {
  const rows = await query("Supabase__execute_sql", {
    query: `select 1 from sent_ledger where item_id = $1 limit 1`, params: [id],
  });
  return Array.isArray(rows) && rows.length > 0;
}
async function recordSent(id) {
  await callToolRetry("Supabase__execute_sql", {
    query: `insert into sent_ledger (item_id, sent_at) values ($1, now())
            on conflict (item_id) do nothing`, params: [id],
  });
}
```

- **Optional: a scheduled prep job.** Pair the dashboard with a job that
  runs ahead of time (a cron, a scheduled task, an edge function) to
  fetch, classify, and pre-draft into the queue table — so when the
  person opens the cockpit the work is already staged and they just
  review. The dashboard then reads the pre-built queue instead of doing
  the heavy scan on open. The job prepares; it still never sends —
  approval stays with the human at the cockpit.

## Build checklist (before you hand it over)

Walk this before declaring the cockpit done:

- [ ] Phase 0 done: you confirmed the JOB and the connector set with the person.
- [ ] Phase 1 done: you called each tool ONCE and wrote down its real shape.
- [ ] The parser handles every envelope you observed (incl. stringified JSON).
- [ ] Fetch-on-open works, caches, and has a reload + visible load/error state.
- [ ] The sender only ever touches `approved` items; `held` is unreachable by it.
- [ ] Default outbound is a draft (reversible) unless the person opted into send.
- [ ] Dedup ledger in place; a double-click / reload cannot double-send.
- [ ] Drafts preserve signature + quoted original, thread correctly, invent nothing.
- [ ] Flagged items show a clear reason and never ship as placeholders.
- [ ] Authoritative systems (CRM) are read-only unless the person said otherwise.
- [ ] View state (sort/filter/collapsed/category) persists across re-open.
- [ ] It's one self-contained HTML file, light mode, approved CDNs only.

## Operating notes

- **Connector-agnostic, always.** Build for what THIS person has
  connected. The examples name real tools only as anchors — a different
  person with HubSpot instead of Attio, or no data source at all, gets a
  cockpit shaped to their tools.
- **Boring by default.** No charting library for a sparkline you can draw
  in 10 lines of SVG. Fewer CDNs = fewer ways for the artifact to break
  offline.
- **The human is the operator, not the obstacle.** Every gate exists so
  the person stays in control of what goes out under their name. Speed
  comes from pre-staging and one-click approval, never from removing the
  human from the send path.
- If you can't build a piece safely (a tool won't reveal its shape, a
  needed connector isn't connected), STOP and say so — see the Completion
  Status Protocol above. A cockpit that half-sends is worse than one you
  flagged as incomplete.
